topic.name: Geriatric Care
objectives: Apply the Beer's Criteria to identify potentially inappropriate medications in older adults
Implement fall risk screening (TUG test, STEADI) and multifactorial prevention strategies
Differentiate types of cognitive impairment (MCI, dementia, delirium) using screening tools
Recognize frailty and sarcopenia using the FRAIL scale and implement management strategies

lessons.title: 💊 Polypharmacy: The American Geriatrics Society Beer's Criteria

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Harold, 82, comes in with his daughter after a fall. She brings a brown paper bag with 14 prescription bottles. 'He's seeing a cardiologist, a urologist, a rheumatologist, and his PCP. I don't think anyone knows everything he's on.' Harold is on amitriptyline (for 'nerve pain'), diazepam (for 'muscle spasms'), diphenhydramine (OTC for sleep), and glipizide (which caused a hypoglycemic last week). Four potentially inappropriate medications — and the fall was predictable. Polypharmacy is the #1 modifiable risk factor for adverse events in older adults.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Drawing of a paper bag overflowing with pill bottles, with warning signs around certain medications

content_chunks.title: Polypharmacy & Beer's Criteria 2023
content_chunks.content:
**Polypharmacy** = ≥5 medications (often associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes)
**Hyperpolypharmacy** = ≥10 medications

**Beer's Criteria 2023 (AGS)**: Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs) to avoid or use with caution in adults ≥65.

**HIGH-RISK PIMs to AVOID** — memorize these for boards:

| Drug | Why Avoid | Better Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| **Anticholinergics** (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, amitriptyline) | Confusion, falls, constipation, urinary retention | Non-sedating antihistamines, gabapentin, topical oxybutynin |
| **Benzodiazepines** (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam) | Falls, cognitive impairment, tolerance, withdrawal | SSRI/SNRI for anxiety, melatonin for sleep |
| **Z-drugs** (zolpidem, zaleplon) | Same fall risk as benzos! | CBT-I, melatonin, trazodone low dose |
| **NSAIDs** (chronic use) | GI bleed, AKI, HTN, HF exacerbation | Acetaminophen, topical analgesics |
| **Sulfonylureas** (glyburide/glibenclamide) | Prolonged hypoglycemia (especially glyburide!) | Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, low-dose glipizide |
| **Skeletal muscle relaxants** (cyclobenzaprine, carisoprodol) | Anticholinergic, sedation, falls | PT, massage, acetaminophen |
| **PPIs** beyond 8 weeks (without indication) | C. diff, osteoporosis, B12 deficiency, CKD | H2 blockers, deprescribe when appropriate |

**Anticholinergic Burden**: Higher total anticholinergic load = more cognitive impairment, falls, mortality.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Table format with three columns: Medication, Why Avoid (with icon), Alternative (green checkmark)

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Deprescribing is a skill**: Don't stop everything at once. Taper benzodiazepines (don't cold-turkey — withdrawal seizures!), stop one drug at a time and monitor. Use the **STOPP/START criteria** alongside Beer's for a comprehensive medication review. And remember: **'Start low, go slow, but GO'** — under-treating is also harmful.

content_chunks.title: Medication Reconciliation: The Brown Bag Review
content_chunks.content:
**Do this at EVERY visit for patients ≥65 on ≥5 meds**:

✅ Ask patient to bring ALL medications (Rx, OTC, supplements, herbals) in a bag
✅ Review each medication for: indication, dose, duration, adherence
✅ Apply **Beer's Criteria** — flag PIMs
✅ Apply **STOPP Criteria** (Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions)
✅ Apply **START Criteria** (Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment) — are they missing indicated meds? (e.g., osteoporosis Tx, statin)
✅ Check for **drug-drug interactions** (use online checker or consult pharmacist)
✅ Check **renal function** — adjust doses for CrCl <30
✅ **One new medication?** Consider stopping an old one (the 'one in, one out' rule)
✅ **Document rationale** for each continued potentially inappropriate medication (shared decision-making)
✅ Set a **deprescribing plan** with timeline and follow-up
content_chunks.visual_desc: Stepwise flowchart showing the brown bag review process with decision points for each medication: Indicated? Effective? Safe? Can we stop/reduce?

quick_checks.q: An 80-year-old man is on amitriptyline 50mg for neuropathy. According to Beer's Criteria, what should you do?
answers: Increase dose for better pain control
Taper and switch to gabapentin or duloxetine
quick_checks.explanation: Amitriptyline is a high-risk anticholinergic per Beer's Criteria. Alternatives for neuropathy include gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine — less anticholinergic burden.

quick_checks.q: Which statement about deprescribing in older adults is TRUE?
answers: Stop all potentially inappropriate medications at once
Taper benzodiazepines gradually to prevent withdrawal
Never stop medications started by a specialist
Supplements don't count in medication review
quick_checks.explanation: Benzodiazepines require gradual tapering to prevent withdrawal seizures/rebound anxiety. Stopping all meds at once is dangerous. Always coordinate with specialists when deprescribing.

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Edna, 78, 'just tripped over the rug' and fractured her hip. She went from independent living to a skilled nursing facility. Six months later, she's still there — deconditioned, depressed, and at high risk for another fall. Falls are the LEADING cause of fatal and non-fatal injuries in adults ≥65. 1 in 4 older adults falls each year. Of those who fall, 50% can't get up without help — leading to 'long lies' (hypothermia, dehydration, rhabdomyolysis). Every well-check includes fall screening for a reason.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Infographic showing the cascade: Fall → Hip fracture → Surgery → Immobilization → Deconditioning → Loss of independence → Nursing home

content_chunks.title: Fall Risk Assessment: STEADI Algorithm
content_chunks.content:
**CDC STEADI** (Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths & Injuries):

**Screen ALL adults ≥65 annually**: "Have you fallen in the past year?"

**If YES**:
→ Assess gait/balance with **Timed Up and Go (TUG)** test
→ Multifactorial risk assessment
→ Individualized intervention

**If NO** but unsteady gait or fear of falling:
→ TUG test + focused prevention

**Timed Up and Go (TUG) Test**:
• Patient stands from chair, walks 10 ft, turns, walks back, sits down
• **Normal**: <12 seconds
• **Impaired**: ≥12 seconds (high fall risk!)
• **Cutoff for frailty**: ≥13.5 seconds

**Other Screening Tools**:
• **Morse Fall Scale**: Inpatient assessment (score ≥45 = high risk)
• **Berg Balance Scale**: 14-item balance assessment (higher score = better)
• **4-Stage Balance Test**: Can they stand with feet side-by-side, semi-tandem, tandem, and single-leg?
content_chunks.mnemonic: **TUG Test**: **T**ime **U**p and **G**o — 12 seconds or more = **F**all risk, **L**ost balance, **A**ssistance needed, **L**ow mobility
content_chunks.visual_desc: Diagram showing TUG test path: Chair → 10 ft walk → Turn → Walk back → Sit. Timer icon showing <12s = normal, ≥12s = fall risk

content_chunks.title: Multifactorial Fall Prevention
content_chunks.content:
**Falls are MULTIFACTORIAL** — address ALL contributing factors:

| Domain | Assess For | Intervention |
|---|---|---|
| **Medications** | Beer's PIMs (benzos, anticholinergics, sedatives, antihypertensives) | Deprescribe, reduce, or substitute |
| **Vision** | Cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, bifocal issues | Ophthalmology referral, update glasses, avoid bifocals when walking |
| **Home hazards** | Throw rugs, poor lighting, cords, clutter, grab bars, railings | Home safety evaluation (OT referral), remove rugs, nightlights |
| **Orthostatic BP** | Check lying + standing BP (drop >20 systolic = abnormal) | Hydrate, reduce antihypertensives, compression stockings |
| **Gait/balance** | TUG test, 4-stage balance test | PT/OT referral, strength training, Tai Chi, walking program |
| **Footwear** | Ill-fitting shoes, barefoot, slippers | Proper footwear with nonslip soles |
| **Bone health** | Osteoporosis screening (DXA) | Calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates if indicated |
| **Vitamin D** | Deficiency common | ≥800 IU/day vitamin D reduces fall risk (USPSTF: clear benefit only with vitamin D + calcium) |

**Hip Fracture Prevention**: Osteoporosis treatment + fall prevention = 50% reduction.

**After a fall**: Assess for injury (X-ray if focal pain, CT head if anticoagulated + head strike), fear of falling (activity restriction causes MORE deconditioning → MORE falls), and consider alert system (Life Alert).
content_chunks.visual_desc: Wheel diagram with 8 spokes: each spoke is a risk domain with assessment tool and intervention

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Orthostatic hypotension is underdiagnosed**: Check orthostatics in EVERY older patient — especially if on antihypertensives, diuretics, or alpha-blockers (tamsulosin!). BP drop >20/10 or symptoms upon standing = abnormal. Don't just check it once; symptoms are often post-prandial (after meals) or in the morning. Also: **Vitamin D 800 IU/day + calcium reduces falls by ~20%** — cheap, safe, effective.

quick_checks.q: A 75-year-old woman completes the TUG test in 15 seconds. What does this indicate?
answers: High fall risk — need multifactorial assessment
quick_checks.explanation: TUG ≥12 seconds = impaired mobility/high fall risk. 15 seconds warrants full multifactorial fall risk assessment and individualized intervention plan.

quick_checks.q: Which of the following is the STRONGEST modifiable risk factor for falls in older adults?
quick_checks.explanation: Medications — particularly benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, and sedatives — are among the strongest modifiable risk factors for falls. Deprescribing these has a major impact.

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Robert, 74, was a retired accountant who 'was always sharp.' His wife noticed he was repeating stories, missing bill payments, and getting lost driving to the grocery store. 'I thought it was just old age,' she said during the visit. It wasn't — it was Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) that progressed to Alzheimer's dementia over 3 years. Differentiating normal aging from MCI from dementia — and frailty from simple deconditioning — determines whether you can intervene early, when treatments matter most.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Three-panel comparison: Normal aging (mild forgetfulness, no functional decline), MCI (noticeable memory changes, preserved function), Dementia (memory + functional decline)

content_chunks.title: Normal Aging vs. MCI vs. Dementia
content_chunks.content:
**Normal Cognitive Aging**:
• Slower processing speed, occasional word-finding difficulty
• **Intact**: Daily function, independence, ability to learn new information
• Memory: Forgets details but recalls later, remembers recent conversations

**Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)** — 'The Gray Zone':
• **Objective cognitive decline** (reported by patient or informant)
• **Preserved functional independence** (can manage meds, finances, driving — just slower/harder)
• Does NOT meet criteria for dementia
• **Subtypes**: Amnestic (memory-predominant) vs. non-amnestic (executive function, language, visuospatial)
• **Progression**: 10-15% per year convert to dementia

**Dementia**:
• Cognitive decline in ≥2 domains (memory, language, executive function, visuospatial)
• **Functional impairment** — CANNOT manage daily activities independently
• Multiple types: Alzheimer's (60-80%), Vascular, Lewy Body, Frontotemporal

**Screening Tools**:
• **Mini-Cog** (3-item recall + clock draw) — 3 minutes, sensitivity 76-99%
• **MoCA** (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) — 10 minutes, more sensitive for MCI
• **SLUMS** (Saint Louis University Mental Status) — good alternative to MMSE
• **MMSE** — widely known but less sensitive for MCI, copyright issues

**When to screen**: Medicare Annual Wellness Visit requires cognitive screening if concerns reported or observed.
content_chunks.mnemonic: **DEMENTIA vs MCI**: Does the patient still **M**anage **C**ash and **I**ndependent living? If **NO** → Dementia. If **YES** → consider MCI.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Venn diagram showing overlap and differences between normal aging, MCI, and dementia with functional independence as key differentiator

content_chunks.title: Frailty: The FRAIL Scale & Sarcopenia
content_chunks.content:
**Frailty** ≠ disability or comorbidity. It's a biologic syndrome of decreased physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors.

**FRAIL Scale** (5 questions, each 1 point):
1. **F**atigue: 'How much of the time did you feel tired in the past month?' (most/all of the time)
2. **R**esistance: Difficulty walking up 10 steps without resting
3. **A**mbulation: Difficulty walking several blocks alone
4. **I**llness: >5 comorbidities
5. **L**oss of weight: >5% body weight in past year

**Score**: 0 = Robust, 1-2 = Pre-frail, ≥3 = Frail

**Sarcopenia** = Age-related loss of muscle mass + strength + function
• **Diagnosis**: Low muscle mass (DXA, BIA, calf circumference <31cm), low handgrip strength (<16kg women, <27kg men), slow gait speed (<0.8 m/s)
• **Consequences**: Falls, fractures, disability, mortality

**Management**:
• **Resistance training** — STRONGEST intervention for sarcopenia (2-3×/week)
• **Protein intake** ≥1.2 g/kg/day (versus 0.8 for younger adults)
• **Vitamin D** ≥800 IU/day
• **Treat underlying causes**: Hypogonadism (testosterone if indicated), thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency
• **Avoid**: Routine use of appetite stimulants (limited evidence, more side effects)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Visual of the FRAIL scale as a 5-rung ladder with icons for each letter, showing progression from robust to frail

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Delirium is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY** — it is NOT dementia! Acute onset, fluctuating consciousness, inattention = delirium until proven otherwise. Common causes: **DELIRIUM** mnemonic = **D**rugs, **E**lectrolyte, **L**ow oxygen, **I**nfection, **R**etention (urinary/fecal), **I**mpaction, **U**ncontrolled pain, **M**etabolic. And **don't miss thyroid** — myxedema coma can present as dementia in older adults.

content_chunks.title: Differential for Cognitive Decline: The 'DEMENTIA' Workup
content_chunks.content:
**Rule OUT reversible causes before diagnosing dementia**:

✅ **Vitamin B12** — deficiency causes reversible cognitive decline
✅ **TSH** — hypothyroidism mimics dementia
✅ **BMP** — electrolyte abnormalities, hypercalcemia, hyponatremia
✅ **Lyme** (if endemic) — neuroborreliosis
✅ **RPR or syphilis screen** — neurosyphilis (rare but reversible)
✅ **CT/MRI head** — rule out: normal pressure hydrocephalus, subdural hematoma, tumor, stroke, extensive white matter disease
✅ **HIV screen** (if risk factors) — HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)
✅ **Medication review** — anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids are COMMON causes of pseudo-dementia
✅ **Depression screening** — pseudodementia of depression (treat depression and cognition improves!)
✅ **Sleep apnea screen** — STOP-BANG questionnaire
content_chunks.visual_desc: Organized checklist with lab tube icons for blood tests and brain icon for imaging, each with checkmark space

quick_checks.q: An 80-year-old man can still manage his finances and medications independently, but his wife reports he repeats stories. What is the MOST likely classification?
quick_checks.explanation: MCI = objective cognitive decline with preserved functional independence. Dementia requires functional impairment (can't manage daily activities). Delirium has acute onset with fluctuating consciousness.

quick_checks.q: According to the FRAIL scale, a patient with a score of 3 out of 5 is classified as:
quick_checks.explanation: FRAIL scale: 0 = Robust, 1-2 = Pre-frail, ≥3 = Frail. Frail patients are at highest risk for falls, hospitalization, and mortality.
